column3: DGS10-DGS2 spread: <0bp next session 100% SHY, >=0bp next session 100% SPY, switch only on the day the sign flips.
column4: 2y and 10y both price Fed-path expectations; a 2/10 inversion is the textbook recession-leading-indicator trigger, and parking in bills while it is negative avoids the growth-scare drawdown in SPY.

column3: Same 2/10 sign-flip trigger as RC001, but the defensive sleeve is TLT instead of SHY.
column4: If the inversion is correctly pricing coming Fed cuts, long-duration TLT should rally on the same cuts that hurt SPY, so duration (not cash) may be the better hedge leg.

column3: DGS10-DGS3MO spread: <0bp next session 100% SHY, >=0bp next session 100% SPY, switch only on sign flip.
column4: 10y-3m is the spread the NY Fed/academic literature finds has the strongest recession-forecasting track record (stronger than 2/10); testing it in the same binary form isolates whether the maturity choice matters.

column3: Same 10y-3m sign-flip trigger as RC003, but the defensive sleeve is TLT instead of SHY.
column4: Pairs with RC002: if duration beats cash as the hedge leg for 2/10, check whether the same holds for the stronger 10y-3m signal.

column3: Only switch to SHY once DGS10-DGS3MO has been continuously <0bp for >=20 consecutive trading days (~1 month); switch back to SPY once the spread is >=0bp for one day (asymmetric: slow in, fast out).
column4: A single-day inversion is noisy (curve dips negative intraday-equivalent then reverts); requiring persistence should cut whipsaw trades versus RC003's day-1 trigger while still catching the sustained-inversion episodes (2000, 2006-07, 2019, 2022-23) that preceded slowdowns.

column3: Same persistence rule as RC005 but the inversion must last >=60 consecutive trading days (~1 quarter) before switching to SHY.
column4: Grid point on the persistence parameter: checks whether a stricter 1-quarter confirmation trades even less often than RC005 and whether that costs or saves excess return (fewer false starts vs later/missed entries).

column3: Same 20-day persistence trigger as RC005, but the defensive sleeve is TLT instead of SHY.
column4: Cross of theme 1/2's duration-vs-cash question with theme 3's persistence filter: does requiring confirmation change which hedge leg (TLT or SHY) works better once the trade is less noisy?

column3: Trigger only on the specific day the curve re-steepens: DGS10-DGS2 had been <0bp for >=20 consecutive trading days and then first prints >=0bp. On that trigger, hold SHY for a fixed 180 trading days, then return to SPY regardless of the spread; ignore the spread during the hold window.
column4: There is a standing market narrative that the un-inversion (not the inversion itself) is the closer-in-time recession/selloff signal, because cuts/flight-to-quality that steepen the curve again often coincide with growth actually breaking down. This design tests that claim directly instead of assuming it, and is scored against RC001/RC005's 'stay defensive while inverted' designs on the same spread.

column3: Same re-steepening trigger logic as RC007 (>=20 consecutive inverted trading days then first >=0bp print) but on DGS10-DGS3MO, with a shorter 120 trading day hold.
column4: Repeats the un-invert-as-signal test on the stronger 10y-3m spread with a shorter hold window, to see if the effect (if any) is sensitive to which curve point or how long the defensive window is held.

column3: Trailing 63-trading-day (~1 quarter) change in DGS10 level: fell >=50bp -> 100% TLT next session; rose >=50bp -> 100% SHY; otherwise 100% IEF. Pure bond rotation, no SPY exposure.
column4: Duration has negative convexity to yield moves: when yields are falling fast, long-duration TLT should outperform; when yields are rising fast, short-duration SHY protects principal; this tests the rate-of-change version of the duration tilt rather than a level threshold.

column3: Same tri-state rotation as RC009 but with a 21-trading-day (~1 month) lookback and a 25bp move threshold instead of 63 days / 50bp.
column4: Grid point on the rate-of-change window: checks whether a faster, more sensitive trigger trades the same duration tilt more often and whether that helps or just adds switching cost.

column3: Level-based (not change-based) tri-state rotation: DGS10 >=4.5% -> 100% SHY next session (avoid duration risk in a high-rate regime); DGS10 <2.5% -> 100% TLT; otherwise 100% IEF.
column4: Contrasts the rate-of-change designs (RC009/RC010) with a pure level view: in a structurally high-rate regime duration risk is larger in absolute terms, in a structurally low-rate regime there is more room for yields to fall and TLT to rally.

column3: Daily effective fed funds rate (DFF): if today's DFF is >=25bp above its value 126 trading days (~6 months) earlier, treat as a hiking cycle and switch SPY to SHY next session; if DFF is flat/falling by that amount, hold/return to SPY.
column4: Hiking cycles tighten financial conditions and historically precede equity drawdowns and credit stress with a lag (2000, 2006-07, 2022); this tests the trend of policy itself, distinct from the curve-shape signals in themes 1-4.

column3: Same hiking-trend rule as RC012 but with a 252-trading-day (~1 year) lookback and 50bp threshold.
column4: Grid point on the FFR-trend lookback: a full-year window should trigger later in a hiking cycle than RC012's 6-month window; compares whether slower confirmation avoids whipsaw at cycle turns (e.g. 2018-19 pause) at the cost of a later defensive entry.
